pages.title: About Green Pulse
pages.content:
Green Pulse is an independent, reader-funded newsroom covering climate, energy and nature. We report on what is happening, explain the numbers behind it and show what people are doing about it, starting with our own streets.

What we believe

Data before drama

Every story links to its sources. When we are unsure, we say so.

Local first

Global change is made of local decisions. We cover both, and the line between them.

Action, not anxiety

Each story ends with something a reader can do, however small.

How we are funded

More than four thousand readers support us with a monthly contribution. We take no money from fossil fuel companies and no advertising from airlines or car makers. Our accounts are published every April.

Corrections

If we get something wrong, we fix it quickly and say what changed at the foot of the story. Write to us through the contact page.

Take action with us
Contact the newsroom

posts.title: Mapping the Heat Islands of Our City
posts.excerpt: Volunteers with cheap thermometers recorded a 7 °C gap between the hottest and coolest streets on the same afternoon. Here is what makes the difference.
posts.content:
On the hottest afternoon of August, forty volunteers cycled set routes across the city with thermometers clipped to their handlebars. By the evening they had logged more than eleven thousand readings, and the map they produced tells a story every planner should see.

7.2 °C

The difference between the hottest car park and the coolest tree-lined street, measured within the same hour.

Source: Green Pulse reader survey, 18 August

What makes a street hot

  • Dark surfaces. Car parks and flat black roofs were consistently the hottest places on the map.
  • No shade. Streets without trees ran 3 to 4 °C hotter than similar streets with a full canopy.
  • Trapped air. Narrow streets with tall buildings held the heat long after sunset.

The good news is that the coolest streets were not the richest ones: they were the ones with mature trees and lighter surfaces. Both are things a city can change within a decade.

The full dataset is open for anyone to download, and the council has agreed to use it when choosing where to plant next winter's two thousand street trees.

comments.author: Lena
comments.content: I did the river route! Amazing to see all the readings come together on one map.

comments.author: Omar
comments.content: Would love to see this repeated next summer to check whether the new trees make a difference.

posts.title: The Street That Built Its Own Solar Farm
posts.excerpt: Sixty households pooled their savings to put panels on a disused field. Two years on, the co-op is paying dividends and cutting bills.
posts.content:
Two years ago, the field at the end of Hawthorn Road was a patch of rough grass behind the bus depot. Today it holds 1,400 solar panels, owned by the people who live a few hundred metres away.

The Hawthorn Energy Co-operative raised its money through community shares: residents bought in from as little as fifty pounds, and a local credit union lent the rest.

1.1 GWh

Electricity generated in the first full year

4.1%

Annual return paid to members

How they did it

  1. A residents' meeting in a church hall, where someone asked who owned the field.
  2. A feasibility study paid for by a small council grant.
  3. A share offer that sold out in nine weeks.
  4. Eight days of installation, with a party on the ninth.

We were tired of waiting for someone else to fix our energy bills. So we became the someone else.

Co-op chair

Surplus income goes into a fund that insulates the homes of members on low incomes. So far, twenty-three homes have been draught-proofed and fitted with new loft insulation.

posts.title: What a Year of River Sampling Revealed
posts.excerpt: Every fortnight for a year, citizen scientists tested the Alder at twelve points. The results show where the pollution comes from, and when.
posts.content:
Every other Sunday morning for a year, small teams of volunteers waded into the River Alder at twelve sampling points and tested the water for nitrates, phosphates and bacteria. They have now published everything they found.

Three findings

  • Phosphate levels spiked within 48 hours of heavy rain at four points downstream of storm overflows.
  • The two stretches with restored riverside trees had the lowest water temperatures all summer.
  • Mayfly larvae, a sign of clean water, returned to three sites where they had not been recorded for a decade.

The group has shared its data with the water company and the environment regulator, and is asking for real-time monitoring at every overflow on the river.

New volunteers are always welcome. Training takes one morning, and the kits are provided.

comments.author: Priya
comments.content: The mayfly news made my week. Thank you to everyone who stood in a cold river for this.

posts.title: A Practical Guide to Cutting Your Home Energy Use by a Third
posts.excerpt: No new boiler, no solar panels: twelve changes, ranked by cost and impact, that together can cut a typical home's energy use by around a third.
posts.content:
Most energy-saving advice is either too vague ("be mindful") or too expensive ("install a heat pump"). This guide sits in between: changes most households can make this winter, ranked by what they cost and what they save.

Free, this weekend

  • Turn the thermostat down by one degree: around 8% less heating energy.
  • Lower the boiler flow temperature to 60 °C or below.
  • Wash clothes at 30 °C and skip the tumble dryer when you can.
  • Close curtains at dusk and open them on sunny mornings.

Under fifty pounds

  • Draught-proof doors, windows and letterboxes.
  • Fit radiator reflector panels on external walls.
  • Insulate the hot water cylinder and exposed pipes.
  • Swap the last old bulbs for LEDs.

−31%

Average fall in energy use across the 48 reader households who tried every free and low-cost step for one winter.

Worth saving for

Loft insulation, cavity wall insulation and a smart thermostat take more money and planning, but they pay back within a few years. Check whether your council or energy supplier offers a grant first.

More action guides

posts.title: Why Our Road Verges Are Turning Wild
posts.excerpt: Mowing less has turned forty kilometres of grass into wildflower meadow. Bees, beetles and some unexpected birds have noticed.
posts.content:
Three summers ago, the county cut back its mowing on forty kilometres of road verge from eight times a year to twice. Residents who complained about the "untidy" grass in the first year are now some of its biggest fans.

What came back

  • Twenty-six species of wildflower, including two orchids
  • Twice as many bumblebees in summer counts
  • Barn owls hunting along the long grass at dusk

Road verges cover a surprising amount of land: across the country they add up to an area larger than many national parks. Managed well, they become corridors that let wildlife move between fragmented habitats.

We did not plant a single seed. We just stopped cutting.

County roads manager

Safety comes first: sight lines at junctions and bends are still cut short. But everywhere else, the verges are being allowed to flower and set seed before the late-summer cut.

comments.author: Gareth
comments.content: We spotted an owl on the bypass verge last week. Never seen one there before.

posts.title: Inside the Repair Café Movement
posts.excerpt: Toasters, lamps and radios get a second life at a monthly repair café, and so does the idea that broken does not mean finished.
posts.content:
On the last Saturday of every month, the library meeting room fills with broken things. A volunteer electrician sits at one table, a seamstress at another, and a retired engineer who can fix almost any radio holds court by the window.

In its first year, the repair café saw 612 items and fixed 71% of them. Each repair kept something out of landfill and, just as importantly, taught its owner a little about how it worked.

612

Items brought in

71%

Fixed on the day

2.4 t

Kept out of landfill

How to start one

  1. Find a free room and a regular date.
  2. Recruit three or four fixers with different skills.
  3. Get basic public liability insurance.
  4. Put the kettle on and let people queue.

Nobody is charged for repairs, though most visitors leave something in the tin for spare parts and biscuits.

posts.title: The Numbers Behind Ocean Plastics
posts.excerpt: How much plastic reaches the sea, where it comes from, and which interventions actually reduce it. A data explainer.
posts.content:
Ocean plastic is one of the most visible environmental problems and one of the most misunderstood. Headlines tend to swing between apocalyptic and dismissive. The data tells a more useful story.

80%

Share of ocean plastic estimated to arrive from land, mostly via rivers, rather than from ships or fishing.

Source: synthesis of published river-flux studies

Where it comes from

The biggest gains come from making sure waste is collected in the first place, especially in fast-growing cities. Clean-ups matter for local wildlife, but they treat the symptom rather than the source.

For individuals, the most effective steps are unglamorous: avoid single-use items where there is a reusable alternative, and support deposit return schemes that put a value on every bottle.

posts.title: Campaign Update: Ten Thousand Trees by Spring
posts.excerpt: The readers' campaign for more street trees has passed its halfway mark. Here is where the money went and what happens next.
posts.content:
In March, Green Pulse readers set themselves a goal: ten thousand new street trees in the city before next spring. As of this week, 5,240 have been planted, funded or promised.

5,240

Trees planted or funded out of the 10,000 target

Where the trees are going

Following the heat island map, the first plantings are focused on the six neighbourhoods with the least canopy cover. Each tree comes with two years of watering by a volunteer street steward.

  • 2,100 trees planted by the council with campaign match funding
  • 1,890 funded by readers and local businesses
  • 1,250 promised by schools and housing associations

For the first time in years, the kids on our estate will grow up under trees.

A street steward

Planting season runs from November to March. You can sponsor a tree, become a steward or nominate your own street.

Join the campaign
Read the heat map story

comments.author: Maya
comments.content: Our school is planting thirty in November. The children have already named them.
